q: Collision theory explains how chemical reactions occur.
e: True. Collision theory explains how chemical reactions occur. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: Collision theory is based on the kinetic molecular theory of solids.
e: False. Collision theory comes from the kinetic molecular theory of gases, where particles fly and collide. Solids do not give that simple colliding-gas picture.

q: Reactant particles moving in random directions possess kinetic energy.
e: True. Reactant particles moving in random directions possess kinetic energy. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: When reactant particles frequently collide with one another, the energy is transferred as a result of the collision.
e: True. When reactant particles frequently collide with one another, the energy is transferred as a result of the collision. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: All collisions between reactant particles result in the formation of reaction products.
e: False. Only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation succeed. Most collisions just bounce off.

q: For a reaction to occur, colliding particles must possess a certain minimum energy known as an activation energy.
e: True. For a reaction to occur, colliding particles must possess a certain minimum energy known as an activation energy. Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.

q: During a collision, the spatial orientation of the reactant molecules is unimportant to determine whether or not a reaction occurs.
e: False. Orientation matters. If the wrong ends hit, even a hard collision can fail.

q: If the colliding particles have the incorrect orientation, they will bounce off each other.
e: True. If the colliding particles have the incorrect orientation, they will bounce off each other. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The unsuccessful collisions with insufficient energy produce a reaction.
e: False. Insufficient energy means the collision is unsuccessful, so no product forms. The particles bounce apart still as reactants.

q: When the particles collide with the correct orientation, they must have enough energy for a successful collision to produce a reaction.
e: True. When the particles collide with the correct orientation, they must have enough energy for a successful collision to produce a reaction. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: The rate of reaction depends on the rate of successful collisions between reactant particles.
e: True. The rate of reaction depends on the rate of successful collisions between reactant particles. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: Reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy to form the activated complex.
e: True. Reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy to form the activated complex. The activated complex is a short-lived, high-energy arrangement that can split to products or fall back to reactants.

q: An activated complex is a permanent species formed by the reactant particles as a result of the collision.
e: False. The activated complex is temporary and unstable. It exists only at the energy peak, then splits to products or back to reactants.

q: The more successful collisions there are, the faster the rate of a reaction.
e: True. The more successful collisions there are, the faster the rate of a reaction. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: Chemical reactions depend on the collisions between the reacting particles such as atoms, molecules or ions.
e: True. Chemical reactions depend on the collisions between the reacting particles such as atoms, molecules or ions. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: Reacting particles must collide in the correct orientation with sufficient energy to overcome the energy barrier to react.
e: True. Reacting particles must collide in the correct orientation with sufficient energy to overcome the energy barrier to react. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: According to the collision theory, a reaction will speed up if the frequency of collision decreases.
e: False. Fewer collisions mean a slower reaction. Rate rises when collision frequency rises.

q: A reaction will speed up if the proportion of particles with energy that is greater than the activation energy increases.
e: True. A reaction will speed up if the proportion of particles with energy that is greater than the activation energy increases. Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.

q: Collision theory can be used to explain the main factors such as concentration, temperature, pressure, and particle size.
e: True. Collision theory can be used to explain the main factors such as concentration, temperature, pressure, and particle size. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: For a chemical reaction to occur, the colliding molecules must possess at least a certain minimum energy necessary to rearrange the original bonds breaking or new bonds forming.
e: True. For a chemical reaction to occur, the colliding molecules must possess at least a certain minimum energy necessary to rearrange the original bonds breaking or new bonds forming. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The activation energy ($E_a$) is the maximum energy that reactant particles must possess for a successful collision.
e: False. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed, not the maximum. Particles need at least Ea, not at most Ea.

q: During the progress of a reaction, an unstable intermediate which is known as an activated complex is formed before producing a product.
e: True. During the progress of a reaction, an unstable intermediate which is known as an activated complex is formed before producing a product. The activated complex is a short-lived, high-energy arrangement that can split to products or fall back to reactants.

q: A hydrogen molecule and an iodine molecule collide to form an unstable intermediate $[H_2I_2]$.
e: True. A hydrogen molecule and an iodine molecule collide to form an unstable intermediate [H2I2]. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: In order to get the product $HI$, the reactants must pass through a short-lived, high-energy transition state.
e: True. In order to get the product HI, the reactants must pass through a short-lived, high-energy transition state. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: The minimum energy that needs to be reached in the transition state is equal to the activation energy ($E_a$) for that reaction.
e: True. The minimum energy that needs to be reached in the transition state is equal to the activation energy (Ea) for that reaction. Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.

q: The activation energy represents an energy barrier for the reaction, and it has the same value in all reactions.
e: False. Ea is a barrier, but every reaction has its own value. Fast reactions have small Ea; slow ones have large Ea.

q: In the reaction between $H_2$ gas and $I_2$ gas to form $HI$, the final product has less energy than the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic.
e: True. In the reaction between H2 gas and I2 gas to form HI, the final product has less energy than the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic. Exothermic means the system releases heat, so delta H is negative.

q: Some energy is absorbed when the activated complex leads to the formation of the products in an exothermic reaction.
e: False. After the peak, an exothermic path drops and energy is released to the surroundings. Absorption on the way down would not be exothermic.

q: When there is sufficient energy to overcome the energy barrier, the formation of the product is favourable.
e: True. When there is sufficient energy to overcome the energy barrier, the formation of the product is favourable. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: If the energy is not enough to overcome the energy barrier, the decomposition of the product back to reactants will occur.
e: True. If the energy is not enough to overcome the energy barrier, the decomposition of the product back to reactants will occur. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: A high $E_a$ means that relatively few collisions have the required energy to produce the activated complex, and hence, the reaction rate is fast.
e: False. A high Ea means few collisions succeed, so the rate is slow. Fast rates go with a low barrier.

q: With a low $E_a$, more collisions have sufficient energy to react, and the reaction rate is fast.
e: True. With a low Ea, more collisions have sufficient energy to react, and the reaction rate is fast. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: A successful collision is a collision that causes a chemical reaction.
e: True. A successful collision is a collision that causes a chemical reaction. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation to react.

q: Transition state is also known as an intermediate state and is a highly energetic state that would be highly unstable.
e: True. Transition state is also known as an intermediate state and is a highly energetic state that would be highly unstable. Transition metals have a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion.

q: The activated complex may form products or break apart to reform the reactants.
e: True. The activated complex may form products or break apart to reform the reactants. The activated complex is a short-lived, high-energy arrangement that can split to products or fall back to reactants.
